caveats: **No sample exercises a real action.** `execute()` returns `error|Echo database not initialized` with rc 1 whenever the plugin's database handle is null, and that handle is opened only by `init()` (through `EchoDatabase::open`), which the `plugin-capture` driver never calls. Every action in the samples above, including `compatibility` which needs no database, fails at that one guard, so the samples show only that the plugin loads.

**`rollup` is Destructive/Irreversible and its output is positional.** `do_rollup` runs `run_retention()`, which permanently deletes aged rows, then the byte budget. Its response is the single line `echo|rollup|0|rows_aggregated` (the count stays for stored clients; nothing is aggregated any more), so the declared `status` column is never populated, and `snapshot` has the same gap (`echo|snapshot|complete` or `partial|<sources>` carries no event count).

**`retention_days` does not set how long data is kept.** The setting is validated, stored and echoed by `status`, but `run_retention` prunes each tier against the window in the schema registry (90 days for hourly, 180 days for daily and a year for monthly; row-count caps on `netqual_boot` and `usage_live`). Changing it alters nothing that is deleted.

**Several legs are declared but have no collector.** `perf` and `procperf` on macOS, `software` on Linux and macOS, `module` on Linux and macOS, and `dns` and `netconn` on Linux and macOS are `planned`: no code path exists for them (confirmed absent in `echo_perf.cpp`, `echo_proc_perf.cpp` and the non-Windows branch of `echo_software_collector.cpp`). A `planned` leg's table is queryable and empty, which means "not yet collecting", never "nothing happened".

**Registry capture stores new values unmasked, and a writer is a lead, not proof.** The new data of every added or changed watched value is readable through `sql` (up to 512 bytes, for example a Winlogon autologon `DefaultPassword` when it changes); the per-key baseline in `echo_state` holds only each value's type, size and an unsalted hash, and the old value is not stored (a baseline written by an older build also holds a rendered prefix of each value until a complete read of that root rewrites it; a key under a subtree the read could not open keeps its earlier entry, and rows an older build wrote were folded by the schema migration, which keeps no old value). The tier keeps the last writer's image when the Kernel-Registry ETW correlation named one; the writer's pid and the attribution detail are not kept (a roll-up has no per-event row to hold them). A value written and reverted between two reads is not recorded, and a profile first seen (at its first logon, or as a logged-off profile first found after an upgrade) is baselined silently at its first read: the upgrade date is the start of offline coverage. A logged-off user's hive is read on the hourly tick (every 12 slow ticks, hourly at the default 300 s; 6 minutes to 24 hours as `slow_interval` varies), unmasked, through the guarded offline-hive mount, for each profile the profile-list walk can resolve a path for (the walk reads at most 512 entries; beyond that the profiles it reaches are read and `registry_offline_discovery_incomplete` stays `1`, and a profile deleted from such a host is never dropped). A profile first found with an absent or unreadable `ProfileImagePath` is not read, and nothing reports it (no health key, row or log line) until a later walk supplies the path; a virtual service or system account is never read; the path that a profile's record lists beside its `<sid>.bak` leftover (a temporary profile) is never mounted: a profile with a known path keeps being read from it, while one with no path yet is not read (a known entry still pathless is counted by `registry_offline_roots_deferred`; a sid first seen beside a stale leftover is reported by nothing while the leftover exists). A path first learned or changed for a known profile is taken only when a second walk in the same tick lists the same path. A change in such a hive is recorded when it is next read, so it may predate the read or the logoff, and it never names a writer: a write the user made just before logging off, and Yuzu's own audited `registry.set_user_value`, look the same, and the tier does not keep the offline marker that would tell the change from a loaded hive's. A refused or failed mount keeps the baseline and counts one gap event per root (up to five per hive); the reason is not stored. The mount holds the profile's `NTUSER.DAT` exclusively for its duration, expected to be short but not measured, and enables the backup and restore privileges, which can fail a logon that races it (the profile may load as a temporary one); a mount that cannot be unloaded leaves the hive locked until it is released (`reg unload`), and the registry source unloads any such leftover `YUZU_HIVE_*` mount, without force, when it starts (one that is refused or fails to unload is logged and left for `reg unload`). Mounts are not audited one by one: the latest read time and status per root are in the `echo_cursor` row.

definitions.description: Internal trigger-driven action that collects process and network connection snapshots, computes diffs against previous state, and records change events. Runs automatically every 60 seconds by default. When a maintenance pass ran out of time with the database still over db_budget_bytes, this action also runs one more bounded eviction slice (at most 2 seconds; the same rows the next timer tick would remove). Not typically invoked manually.

Internal trigger-driven action that collects service and user session snapshots, computes diffs against previous state, and records change events. Also checks if purge is due and removes expired records. Runs automatically every 300 seconds by default. Not typically invoked manually.

Returns the live OS-support matrix for every Echo capture source. Output is one header line followed by N row lines, pipe-delimited: header|source|os|status|capture_method|notes row|process|windows|supported|toolhelp32|... row|process|linux|supported|procfs|... Status values: supported | constrained | planned | unsupported. Use this to verify on a target host which capture sources are wired and which are kPlanned (so operators can pre-stage network_capture_method before the implementation lands). Read-only, static metadata — does not touch the database or the filesystem, safe to call at any frequency.

Updates Echo plugin configuration. Changes take effect on the next collection cycle. Configurable settings include data retention period, the database byte budget, collection intervals, and command-line redaction patterns for sensitive data protection. Lowering db_budget_bytes deletes history on the next maintenance pass (within 15 minutes) and cannot be undone.

Show all TCP connections to a specific remote IP address. Replace the target_ip parameter with the IP to investigate. A socket first seen already closing is recorded once per process and remote per hour, so it appears once here and never as a disconnect.

Show daily aggregated TCP connection counts by remote address and process. A socket first seen already closing is recorded once per process and remote per hour, so it appears once here and never as a disconnect.

Per-day process activity for the last 30 days, aggregated from $Process_Daily. Each row is (date, process_name, user, start_count, stop_count). Useful for trend questions ("did $process_name run more often last week than the week before?") that would be O(N) over $Process_Hourly.

Exports Echo events as a JSON array for integration with external analytics tools (Splunk, ClickHouse, ELK). Each event object includes id, timestamp, event_type, event_action, snapshot_id, and a nested detail object with type-specific fields.

Produces a single JSON document enumerating every running process and open network connection on this host at the moment of invocation, in the fleet_snapshot.v1 schema. Used by the server-side FleetTopologyStore to assemble the 3D fleet network-topology view (/viz/fleet, ladder PR 5+). Each list is capped at 4096 entries; truncation is signalled by truncated_processes and truncated_connections flags. Cmdlines are redacted per the active redaction_patterns config (defaults always apply). Process and tcp source pause states are honoured -- when paused, the corresponding list is empty and source_paused.* markers appear in the payload. Not typically invoked manually; the server pulls on demand at the topology cache TTL.
Show hourly aggregated process start counts for the last 7 days.

Show the TCP ports that opened a listening socket, with the owning process and how many listening sockets opened and closed, from the hourly roll-up. The roll-up keeps counts per hour, not a list of the sockets open right now, and no pid.

Show the processes started in the last complete hour and the current one with the name of their parent, from the hourly roll-up (a bucket is keyed by its start, so the window reaches back two hours). The roll-up keeps names and counts per hour, not pids, so the tree is by parent name.

Queries the Echo hourly roll-up for system activity within a time range. Echo keeps hourly, daily and monthly roll-up tiers only, so each row is one hour bucket of one capture source: process starts/stops, network connections opened/closed, service state changes, and user logins/logouts are counted per hour, not listed one by one. Results are pipe-delimited: timestamp|event_type|event_action|snapshot_id|detail_json, where timestamp is the bucket start, event_action is always bucket and snapshot_id is 0. The detail_json field contains a JSON object holding that bucket's key fields and counts, named as the columns of the source's hourly table are (for example name, user, start_count and stop_count for a process). For anything finer than that, or for daily and monthly figures, use echo.sql over the $<Source>_Hourly, $<Source>_Daily and $<Source>_Monthly tables.

Recent ARP / neighbour-table activity (ADR-0015) — IP<->MAC bindings per interface with their appeared and removed counts per hour, from the hourly roll-up. Requires the `arp` capture source to be enabled on the device (the default).

Recent DNS resolver-cache state (ADR-0015) — name/record_type/data with their appeared and removed counts per hour, from the hourly roll-up. Device-level (no per-process attribution). Requires the `dns` capture source to be enabled on the device (the default).

Mapped network-share activity (capability-map §3.8) in both directions — outbound (drives this host maps to remote shares) and inbound (remote hosts mapping this host's shares), as appeared and removed counts per hour from the hourly roll-up. Mappings found by the one-time historical backfill (registry / fstab / event-log) are counted in historical_count. Requires the `mapdrive` capture source to be enabled on the device (the default); rows expose share paths.
Show process starts and stops per hour for the last 24 hours, from the hourly roll-up.

Same as `echo.recent_processes` but emits human-readable ISO-8601 timestamps via `datetime(hour_ts, 'unixepoch')` instead of epoch seconds. Use this when piping query output to a human reader; use `echo.recent_processes` when piping to another tool that expects epoch seconds.

Force an immediate maintenance pass (normally runs every 15 minutes). Permanently deletes rows older than each tier's retention limit, and then enforces the database byte budget (db_budget_bytes): while the database is over it, the pass permanently deletes hourly rows older than 48 hours (5 days for procperf), even inside their retention window; paused or errored sources (an unreadable <source>_enabled counts as errored) are exempt. It may also run the one-off VACUUM that converts an older database to incremental auto_vacuum (collectors, status and configure wait while it runs). Classified Destructive/Irreversible with no approval gate: an operator who can dispatch it deletes history immediately and cannot undo it.
Show recent service state changes per hour, from the hourly roll-up.

Forces an immediate full snapshot of all four Echo collectors (processes, network connections, services, user sessions). Computes diffs against the previous state and records any detected changes. Useful before maintenance windows or incident investigations.

Execute an arbitrary SELECT query against the Echo warehouse tables on each targeted agent. Use $-prefixed table names ($Process_Hourly, $TCP_Daily, etc.) which are translated to real table names on the agent. Only SELECT queries are permitted.

Returns the current status of the Echo database including record count, oldest and newest event timestamps, the database size (used pages plus the write-ahead log), and the configured retention period. Use this to verify Echo is collecting data and to monitor disk usage. Also reports both the configured network_capture_method and the network_capture_method_effective (the mechanism actually collecting — always polling today), so status never misrepresents the active capture mechanism. On the healthy path the FIRST line is storage_state|ok. Offline means collection and retention are both stopped until the agent restarts and every other field is withheld -- the reply is then just an error| line followed by storage_state|offline (a wedged rollback closed the Echo database) or storage_state|offline|free_space (the roll-up migration was refused at start because the volume held less than twice the database file plus its write-ahead log free, or its free space could not be read; the file is untouched and Echo loads without its database until a restart with the space freed), and the action exits non-zero. The order is REVERSED on that path: error| comes FIRST, because server and dashboard consumers key off the output starting with error|, so do not assume storage_state is always the first line. Historical data NORMALLY stays queryable via echo sql, but only when the read-only query connection is itself available; the error| line states which case applies, so do not infer echo sql access from storage_state|offline alone. Reports the retention clock guard counters (#2361): retention_guard_declines_total and retention_guard_failures_total are always present, with per-table retention_guard|<table>|<n> and retention_guard_failed|<table>|<n> lines for any table with a non-zero count (retention_guard|__budget__|<n> is not a table: the byte-budget pass was skipped because the retention clock guard refused this pass's clock; it is counted in neither total). Read the two totals TOGETHER - a zero declines total only means the endpoint's clock is behaving if the failures total is also zero. Scrape this across the fleet to find hosts whose clocks need attention; the agent has no /metrics endpoint. Reports the byte budget: db_budget_bytes (the configured cap; unknown when the setting could not be read, in which case that pass is skipped and retried), budget_over_bytes (how far used pages plus the write-ahead log sit above the budget when status runs, measured then and not cached from the last pass; 0 within budget, unknown when the size or the setting cannot be read; above 0 while an echo.sql read pins the log, after an eviction pass that failed or was skipped, while a catch-up is still draining, or when only exempt rows remain), budget_evicted_hourly_rows_total (cumulative hourly rows the budget removed; budget_evicted_raw_rows_total is retired, no longer written, and prints its last value for one release), and db_auto_vacuum (incremental; none; or deferred once a one-off conversion was wanted and could not run, for too little free disk space or a failed VACUUM, which stays until a conversion succeeds). Per capture source it reports config|<src>_rows|<n>, the rows held for that source (an agent from before the roll-up-only release reports config|<src>_live_rows|<n> instead; the server shows a dash for it rather than reading that figure as the hourly count). module_dedup_overflow_total and tcp_closing_dedup_overflow_total count how often the hourly de-duplication sets filled and were cleared. An exception inside any action ends the reply with a fixed error|internal line and exit code 1; it can follow lines already written, so a consumer must not assume error| is first on that path; the cause is in the agent log.

Aggregate TCP connections grouped by process name and remote endpoint. A socket first seen already closing is recorded once per process and remote per hour, so it appears once here and never as a disconnect.
Show recent user logins and logouts per hour, from the hourly roll-up.

description: Echo activity record -- continuous system state change tracking
how_it_works:
Echo is the agent's local telemetry warehouse. Each capture source has a collector that reads current
OS state on a timer, compares it with the baseline saved at the previous tick and folds only the
differences, as change events, into hourly, daily and monthly roll-up tiers in a SQLite database
(`echo.db`) on the device. Four interval triggers run the collectors and a fifth trims every tier to
its limit, holds the database to its byte budget and sweeps the string dictionary. Three sources (`power`, `removable`, `registry`) do not diff a
snapshot: they follow a saved position in an OS log or callback stream, and when that position is
lost they record a `capture_gap` row and start again from the log's current end instead of replaying
history. All 17 sources are on by default on every OS (`default_enabled` in `echo_schema_registry.cpp`,
enforced by a registry-wide test). `configure` turns any of them off per host, which stops capture
and keeps the rows already stored; `purge_source` then deletes that source's rows. Reads are on
demand and local: `status`, `query`, `export` and `sql` read `echo.db`, `snapshot` forces an
out-of-cycle collection, and `fleet_snapshot` re-enumerates processes and connections without
touching `echo.db`.

Storage model: roll-up is the only one, and no setting, flag or mode selects another. Every event is
folded, in one transaction with its baseline, into an interned string dictionary (`echo_dict`) and
one physical table per source and tier (`<source>_<tier>_r`), read through a view of the tier's own
name (`process_hourly`, `tcp_daily`, ...). Counts and sums add, maxima and minima keep the extreme,
and a "last" value keeps the newest. The usage fold rides the process fold's transaction, so a
failure of either rolls back both. Raw capture rows are not kept: what an event leaves behind is the
keys and measures its tier declares, so a per-event pid, command line or timestamp cannot be read
back. `echo.sql` reads the tiers directly; `echo.query` and `echo.export` return the hourly buckets
as rows of the old shape. The retired raw names (`$Process_Live`
and the other fifteen `<source>_live`) stay answerable as empty views with their old columns, so a
stored query returns no rows instead of an error. A database written by an earlier build is migrated
once, in a single transaction, on the first open (schema v10; see "Upgrading an existing
database"): the volume must hold twice the database file plus its write-ahead log free, or the open is refused with the
retired tables intact and Echo stays offline (`status` reports `storage_state|offline|free_space`)
until space is freed and the agent restarts. `sql` refuses common table expressions (`WITH`; a query that starts with `WITH` gets
`only SELECT queries are allowed`), `NATURAL` / `USING` joins (write joins with `ON`) and
bound-parameter markers, and reads only through the tables and views the schema lists.

Deliberately not: Echo does not stream events to the server in real time (everything lands in the
local warehouse first and is pulled by a read action), it does not replay history from zero when a
cursor-model source loses its position, and it never fabricates OS support (a leg with no collector
reports `planned`, not a guessed read).

| Trigger | Default cadence | Action | What it drives |
|---|---|---|---|
| `echo.fast` | 60 s (10-3600) | `collect_fast` | `process`, `tcp`, `arp`, `dns`, `netqual`, `module` and the derived `usage` fold |
| `echo.slow` | 300 s (30-7200) | `collect_slow` | `service`, `user`, `netconn`, `mapdrive` and the cursor sources `power`, `removable`, `registry` |
| `echo.perf` | 30 s | `collect_perf` | `perf`, `procperf` (device and per-application counters, sampled rather than diffed) |
| `echo.software` | 3600 s (0 removes the trigger, otherwise 300-86400) | `collect_software` | `software` |
| `echo.rollup` | 900 s | `rollup` | retention of the tiers, then the byte budget and file hygiene, then the weekly dictionary sweep |

The fast interval must stay below the slow interval. A diffed source's first tick records its baseline and
no events, so a quiet first tick is not evidence about the past.

### What you can decide with it

| Question | Use | What you get, and the limit |
|---|---|---|
| Is Echo healthy on this device? | `status` | Storage state, row counts, per-source `last_status`, `consecutive_failures` and `last_status_at`, and the retention clock-guard counters. `status` is the only fleet-readable health signal (the agent has no `/metrics` endpoint for Echo). |
| What can this OS do? | `compatibility` | One row per source and OS, with status `supported`, `constrained`, `planned` or `unsupported` and the capture method. |
| What ran, and when did it start or stop? | `query type=process`, `recent_processes`, `process_tree`, `hourly_process_summary`, `daily_process_summary` | Windows records start and stop from a gap-free ETW stream, names only. Linux polls `/proc` every fast interval and keeps the command line (redacted by pattern), so a process shorter than the interval can be missed. macOS uses Endpoint Security when root and the entitlement are present and a poll otherwise, names only. |
| Who talked to this address, and what is listening? | `connections_to_ip`, `tcp_by_process`, `listening_ports`, `daily_connection_summary` | Polled connection tables on every OS; a connection that opens and closes inside one interval is not seen. macOS sees every flow only with root. |
| Did a service change state, who logged on? | `service_state_changes`, `user_sessions` | Windows is complete. Linux and macOS are constrained: no start type, and `utmp` or `utmpx` can miss GUI logins and containers without them. |
| Which software was installed or removed? | `query type=software` | Windows only (machine-wide Uninstall keys). Empty on Linux and macOS means not collected. |
| Did a persistence or policy registry value change? | `sql` over `$Registry_Hourly` (`$Registry_Live` answers no rows) | Windows only. The newest data of each changed value (up to 512 bytes, unmasked, as `last_data`), its type and the image of the writing process when attributed (`last_actor_image`); the old value is not kept. A logged-off user's change is counted in the same tiers and never names a writer. |
| Did the device sleep, wake, change power source, or have media attached? | `sql` over `$Power_Hourly`, `$Removable_Hourly` | `capture_gap` rows mark any stretch the agent could not see. |
| Who is on the network segment, what did it resolve, which shares are mapped? | `recent_arp`, `recent_dns`, `recent_mapdrive`, or `query` with type arp, dns or mapdrive | `dns` is Windows only; `mapdrive` outbound live only on macOS. These are device-state sources: they are never part of the default `query` feed. |
| Anything else in the warehouse | `sql` | A single SELECT against `$`-prefixed tables, validated by `validate_and_translate_sql` and run through the read-only `execute_user_query`. The `usage` tables are not queryable here. |
| Pull a time range out for another tool | `export` | JSON array of events, same filters as `query`. `limit` defaults to 1000; a value above 10000 (or zero or less) falls back to 1000. |

What a result proves. A row says the collector saw that change at that tick; it does not say nothing
else happened. An empty table on a `planned` leg means Echo is not collecting there, never that
nothing occurred. An empty table on a live leg can also mean the source is disabled (check
`<source>_enabled` in `status`), the first tick was a baseline, or the last tick reported
`capture_incomplete`. `snapshot` answers `complete` or `partial|<sources>`; a partial answer names
the sources that kept a stale baseline.

Safe workflow for the changing actions:

1. `configure` (Write, admin only): run `compatibility` and `status` first, apply the setting, then
   read `status` again. The setting is undone by writing the old value back; rows already stored are
   not touched, and re-enabling a source re-baselines it so nothing is invented for the paused
   window.
2. `purge_source` (Delete, irreversible): `export` what you need, disable the source with
   `configure`, run `purge_source`, then confirm with `status` that its row count is zero. It accepts
   only a registered source name that is confirmed disabled.
3. `rollup` (Delete, irreversible): runs by itself every 900 s; a manual run only brings that
   same pass forward. The server refuses to dispatch a Destructive action fleet-wide, so
   both `rollup` and `purge_source` need explicit device ids.

### Capture sources by OS

`live` means the collector is wired and is the primary mechanism; `constrained` means it works with
a stated limit; `planned` means the leg is declared with no collector (its tables are queryable and
empty); `n/a` means the source does not apply to that OS. The table is read from the schema registry
(`build_sources()` in `echo_schema_registry.cpp`); `compatibility` reports the same data on a host.

| Source | Records | Windows | macOS | Linux |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `process` | process start and stop | live: ETW, poll fallback | constrained: Endpoint Security (root and entitlement), else poll | live: procfs |
| `tcp` | TCP and UDP connection changes | live: iphlpapi poll | constrained: nstat (root), else `proc_pidfdinfo` poll | live: procfs poll |
| `service` | service state changes | live: SCM | constrained: `launchctl`, no start type | constrained: `systemctl`, start type `unknown`, systemd only |
| `user` | logon sessions | live: WTS | constrained: `utmpx` | constrained: `utmp` |
| `perf` | device CPU, memory, disk, network rates | live: kernel counters | planned | live: procfs |
| `procperf` | top-N per-application CPU and memory | live: `NtQuerySystemInformation` | planned | live: procfs, version empty |
| `netqual` | per-connection TCP quality | constrained: TCP ESTATS, elevated agent only | constrained: nstat, root only | live: netlink `INET_DIAG` |
| `module` | image and driver loads with signing verdict | live: ETW | planned | planned |
| `software` | installed-software changes | live: HKLM Uninstall keys | planned | planned |
| `arp` | neighbour-table changes | live: `GetIpNetTable2` | constrained: `entry_type` always `unknown` | live: `/proc/net/arp`, IPv4 |
| `dns` | resolver-cache changes | live: DNS client cache | planned | planned |
| `netconn` | connectivity transitions | live: event logs, backfills history | planned | planned |
| `mapdrive` | mapped network shares, both directions | live: outbound, history and inbound (inbound needs local admin) | constrained: outbound live only | constrained: mounts and fstab, inbound needs Samba |
| `power` | sleep, wake, AC transitions (cursor) | constrained: power broadcast | live: `pmset -g log` replay | constrained: logind, needs the libsystemd build, AC read always |
| `removable` | media attach and detach, exec from removable (cursor) | live: event-log channels | constrained: DiskArbitration | constrained: udev netlink |
| `registry` | registry value and key changes (cursor) | live: `RegNotifyChangeKeyValue`; logged-off profiles on the hourly tick (every 12 slow ticks, hourly at the default 300 s) via the guarded hive mount | n/a | n/a |
| `usage` | per-executable runs, derived from `process` | live | constrained: inherits `process` | live |

### Source notes

- **Retention.** The roll-up tiers are time-based, cut by bucket start: 90 days hourly, 180 days
  daily and a year monthly (`usage_daily` keeps 31 days); `netqual_boot` and `usage_live` are
  row-count capped. Each pass deletes at most 5000 rows per table, and a disabled source's rows are
  never pruned.
- **Byte budget.** `db_budget_bytes` (default 250 MiB, minimum 32 MiB) caps used pages plus the
  write-ahead log. Lowering it deletes history on the next maintenance pass (within 15 minutes) and
  cannot be undone: it permanently deletes the oldest eligible history before its tier's retention
  limit, and raising it again does not restore it. The setting is reversible and gated like every
  other `configure` key; the deletion is the maintenance pass's, which is classified destructive. It applies to an existing `echo.db` on upgrade too (the user manual,
  "Upgrading an existing database"). Over budget, the rollup pass removes hourly rows older than
  48 hours (5 days for `procperf`), largest table first, oldest bucket first. There is no raw tier
  to take first. Daily and monthly rows, the `usage` tables, `netqual_boot`, paused or errored
  sources (an unreadable `<source>_enabled` counts as errored) and an unusable `db_budget_bytes`
  value (read as unknown, never as the default) are never touched. A pass is batches of 1,000 rows, each in one transaction with its
  persisted counter, and stops after 2 seconds; while still over budget each fast tick runs another
  slice. The budget is hard for eligible data pages (the pass stops only at the target) and soft for
  the log: a long `sql` read pins the log, exempt rows can hold used pages above the target, and
  `budget_over_bytes` reports the overage. After a pass, free pages are returned
  (`incremental_vacuum(256)`) and the log is checkpointed. A database created before
  `auto_vacuum=INCREMENTAL` is converted by one `VACUUM` once used pages are at or under the target
  (the budget less the 16 MiB log allowance), or once eviction has nothing left to take, and the free
  pages are at least 32 MiB and a quarter of the file; it needs twice the used size free on the
  volume and otherwise reports `db_auto_vacuum|deferred`, retried at most daily.
- **What a tier counts.** `tcp`: a socket first seen already closing counts as one connection per
  process and remote per hour; for outbound connections the hourly `connect_count` for these sockets
  is distinct remotes per process per hour, and an inbound socket first seen closing counts once per
  client socket per hour, because the remote port is the client's ephemeral port. A connection
  attempt that vanishes while its last observed state is `SYN_SENT` counts as `failed`, which can
  over-count a very short-lived connection a poll never saw established; a listening socket counts as
  `listen_open` / `listen_close` under `remote_addr='*'`, never as a connection. `module` (Windows):
  unloads are not counted, risky loads always are, and every other load is counted once per hour per
  loader, module and folder, so `load_count` is distinct combinations for ordinary modules; an image
  with no embedded signature is looked up in the system catalogs (a lookup error reads `unknown`,
  never risky). `registry`: the last value keeps its first 512 bytes, the old value is not kept,
  `bam\State` is excluded and the last-write time of the key is the event time. `echo_state` is
  rewritten only when a baseline changed.
- **`netconn` and `power`/`removable` history.** On first enablement the read can reach back into
  OS-retained history, bounded by `netconn_lookback_seconds`, `power_lookback_seconds` (effective on
  macOS only) and `removable_lookback_seconds` (default 7 days, `0` means forward-only). If the
  setting cannot be read, Echo reads forward-only.
- **`mapdrive` history backfill.** A one-time historical pass runs at agent init. A profile it could
  not read is retried individually, at most 7 attempts in total and no more than once per 24 hours,
  until it resolves or is abandoned. A hive mount that exceeds its 30 s bound ends that run's
  mounting. The stuck mount's thread cannot be stopped: until it returns it keeps the process-wide
  offline-hive lock (every other per-user hive read on the agent waits behind it) and keeps the
  backup and restore privileges enabled on the agent process, and if it stalls after the hive has
  loaded, that hive stays mounted and the profile's `NTUSER.DAT` stays locked. The plugin module is
  pinned in memory before the first mount; if the pin fails no hive is read, and while a stuck
  mount is still running later runs do not start new mounts. `purge_source mapdrive` also clears the
  pending-retry list so a retry cannot re-insert purged rows.
- **`registry`.** The last value is kept unmasked, with its type and the last writer's image; the
  writer's pid and the attribution detail are not kept in the tier; see Caveats. The hives of logged-off users whose profile path the walk can resolve are read on the hourly tick (every 12 slow ticks: hourly at the default 300 s, between 6 minutes and 24 hours as `slow_interval` varies; a hive that is capped, deferred or owed a retry is mounted again on the next tick) through the guarded offline-hive mount: one mount per hive, loaded roots first and the hives in the budget that is left (the tail of a long list is read over the following ticks, visible as `registry_offline_roots_deferred`). A change found there is counted in the same tiers as a loaded hive's and never names a writer; the offline marker is not retained. A refused or failed mount counts one gap event per root (up to five per hive). Discovery walks the profile list with its 512-entry cap: beyond it the profiles the walk reaches are read and `registry_offline_discovery_incomplete` stays `1`. See Caveats.

### Diagrams

#### Dispatch and read path

Operators reach the plugin through the server, which authorizes and audits the dispatch. The
triggers call the same entry point inside the agent. Every action except `fleet_snapshot` works on
`echo.db`, and every result comes back as a normal instruction response.

#### Collector pipeline and retention

Collectors fold only the difference from the last complete snapshot, and a failed or partial read
keeps the old baseline rather than inventing events. Every tier is written as the event arrives, so
retention trims each tier independently. The clock guard declines a time-based pass
that looks like a wall-clock jump (a pass that would wipe a table, more than 30 days since the last
pass, a stored reading ahead of now, or no stored reading) and counts it in
`retention_guard_declines_total`. It declines once per distinct anomaly: while the same anomaly
persists, later passes delete again but never more than 5000 rows per table per pass. Row-count
trimming needs no clock and is not clock-guarded, though it has the same per-pass cap. The byte budget
runs after retention: it is size-triggered, not clock-triggered, it is skipped for a pass on which the
clock guard declined or failed, and it only takes hourly rows. Its 48 h (5 days for `procperf`) floor
does move with a clock error (a clock set forward admits more rows); what bounds what it deletes is the
measured size overage, since the pass stops at the target. A catch-up slice that finds the clock stepped
back below the reading it was admitted with stops instead of deleting (`docs/clock-guarded-retention.md`).

#### Disable, then purge a source

The enable check and the delete happen under the same collector lock that `configure` takes, so a
concurrent re-enable cannot slip between them and have a collecting source purged. An unreadable
flag is treated as unconfirmed and refused, never as disabled. The best-effort truncation of the
SQLite write-ahead log (WAL) clears the purged pages from that log so the erasure is complete.

#### Cursor source states

`power`, `removable` and `registry` keep one saved position each in the `echo_cursor` table (readable
through `sql`). A transient read failure raises an incomplete-capture error (`IncompleteCaptureError`), which keeps the cursor so
the next tick retries from the same place. A lost cursor or wrapped log writes a single
`capture_gap` row and re-baselines at the log's current end, never a replay from zero, and the
window of a disable is likewise reported only as a gap, never as its own events.

inputs.description: Enable or disable the Windows registry change source (registry → $Registry_Hourly and $Registry_Daily; cursor-model seam). **ON by default ("true")**, like every other capture source. Windows only; on Linux and macOS the source is listed as unsupported and records nothing. A curated watch list (Run and RunOnce, Services, Image File Execution Options, AppInit_DLLs, Winlogon, LSA, Policies and Defender under HKLM, plus Run, RunOnce, Policies and Winlogon under each user profile hive the agent can resolve a path for, loaded or unloaded: an unloaded hive is found through the profile list, which is walked up to 512 entries) is watched for changes; each added or changed value is recorded with its new value (up to 512 bytes of text) and its type, a removed value by its name, and each row carries the image of the process that wrote it when attribution succeeded; the old value is not kept, neither its text nor its type or size. VALUES ARE STORED UNMASKED: the newest value of every value added or changed under a watched key is readable through echo.sql as last_data in $Registry_Hourly and $Registry_Daily, for the tier's retention (for example a Winlogon autologon DefaultPassword when it changes). A value that has not changed is not: the per-key baseline in echo_state holds only its type, size and an unsalted hash. The source's cursor row (echo_cursor) holds the new value of a change still waiting for its writer. A baseline written by an older build also holds up to 512 bytes of each value it saw until a complete read of that root rewrites it (a key under a subtree the read could not open keeps its earlier entry), and a cursor row built from one also holds the old value until that change is written (the next slow tick at most). Treat all three accordingly, or set "false" to opt out. The acting process is CORRELATED to each change from a write-only Kernel-Registry ETW session (value writes, value deletions and key deletions) by value name, type, size and time window: the collector names the single process that made a matching write, which is a lead to verify against $Process_Hourly, not proof, and the tier keeps its image as last_actor_image. How the writer was settled (correlated, ambiguous, none, degraded, no session, lost across a restart, or read offline) and the writer's process id are not stored. The ETW session needs an elevated agent; without one no writer is named and the key watch alone runs. The roots of a logged-off user's unloaded hive have no watch: they are read on the hourly tick (every 12 slow ticks, hourly at the default 300 s; sooner on first sight, after a re-enable and every tick while a read is capped or owed a retry) through the guarded offline-hive mount, never naming a process. A change found there is counted in $Registry_Hourly and $Registry_Daily like one from a loaded hive; that it came from an offline read is not retained, and it may predate the read or the logoff. A change is read at the slow tick that sees it (every slow_interval, 300 s by default) and its row lands in that tick once its writer is settled, or in the next one when the write was within a few seconds of the tick or was found by the full re-read of every watched key (every 12 slow ticks, hourly at the default). A change whose writer cannot depend on a later event (no ETW session, a restart, an offline read) is written in the tick that sees it, never held. A value written and reverted between two reads is not recorded. A key is baselined silently at its first read, so for a user hive first seen at logon anything written to its watched keys before that first read is not a row; a user's baseline carries across logoff and logon, so a change made while they were logged off is reported by the next read. Rows live in $Registry_Hourly and $Registry_Daily: the newest value of each changed value is readable there as last_data, unmasked, for the tier's retention (90 days hourly, 180 days daily by default; time-based, not a row count). Setting "false" pauses capture and a later "true" re-baselines every watched key (no row is invented for what changed while paused). Requires an agent newer than v0.14.1; older agents silently ignore. Valid: "true" | "false".
inputs.name: registry_enabled

outputs_note:
Every action writes its response as a sequence of independent lines (one `ctx.write_output` call
per line); most, but not all, actions follow the plugin-wide `discriminator\|field\|field...`
pipe-delimited convention (see `echo_status_format.hpp` and `echo_collectors.hpp`). The four
collection actions share one line shape, `echo\|collect_<leg>\|<events_recorded>\|<token>`, where
`<token>` is one of `source_disabled`, `unsupported_platform`, `baseline`, `sample_recorded`,
`apps_recorded`, `cursor_advanced`, `cursor_lost`, `capture_incomplete`, `counters_unavailable`, `state_unreadable` (the `kCollectStatus*` tokens in `echo_collectors.hpp`; `state_unreadable` is emitted by `skip_token()` in `echo_plugin.cpp`). Cursor sources (`power`, `removable`, `registry`) add their own `echo|collect_<source>|<n>|<token>` line to the `collect_slow` stream.
`status`'s wire format is line-oriented `key\|value` pairs (`storage_state\|ok`,
`record_count\|<n>`, `config\|<key>\|<value>`, ...), not one positional row — the five YAML columns
below correspond to five of those lines; the rest (`config\|*`, `retention_guard\|*`,
`retention_guard_failed\|*`) are operational fields the YAML schema does not model. `query`'s rows
match its five columns exactly, followed by an un-modelled `total\|<n>` summary line. `sql` (and
every canned query in `echo_warehouse.yaml`) emits a leading `__schema__\|<col>\|<col>...` line,
then one pipe-joined data line per row, then a trailing `__total__\|<n>` line — all three land in
the single declared `output` column. `snapshot`'s and `rollup`'s actual lines do not decompose into
their declared columns at all; see Caveats.



**Actions without a definition.** `collect_perf` writes `echo\|collect_perf\|<n>\|<token>`, the same
shape as `collect_fast`/`collect_slow` (see `do_collect_perf` in `echo_plugin.cpp`). `collect_software` follows the
same convention. A failed perf/procperf counter read reports `counters_unavailable` where the registry lists the OS as supported and `unsupported_platform` where it has no perf collector. `status` additionally emits `db_budget_bytes|<n|unknown>` (`unknown`: the setting could not be read, so that pass is skipped and retried), `budget_over_bytes|<n|unknown>` (measured when `status` runs, not cached from the last pass; `unknown` when the size or the setting cannot be read), `budget_evicted_raw_rows_total|<n>`, `budget_evicted_hourly_rows_total|<n>`, `db_auto_vacuum|<incremental|none|deferred>`, `module_dedup_overflow_total|<n>`, `tcp_closing_dedup_overflow_total|<n>`, `db_health|<ok|quarantined>|<epoch>`, `config|perf_capture_method|<m>`, `config|procperf_procs_seen|<n>` and, per capture source, `config|<src>_last_status|<token>`, `config|<src>_consecutive_failures|<n>` and `config|<src>_last_status_at|<epoch>` (process memory only; see the user manual). A failed baseline-only save emits `error|<source> state_save_failed`. `retention_guard|__budget__|<n>` is not a table: the byte-budget pass was skipped because the retention clock guard refused this pass's clock; it is counted in neither `retention_guard_declines_total` nor `retention_guard_failures_total`. An exception inside any action ends the reply with a fixed `error|internal` line and exit code 1; it can follow lines already written, so a consumer must not assume `error|` is first on that path; the cause is in the agent log. `purge_source` writes a single JSON line,
`{"source":"<name>","rows_deleted":<n>,"status":"purged","dictionary_pending":<true|false>}` (see `do_purge_source` in `echo_plugin.cpp`), or an
`error|` line if the named source is unknown, still enabled, or its enable flag cannot be read (`config_unreadable`).
`dictionary_pending` is `true` when the dictionary sweep that follows the row delete (the interned strings only the
purged rows referenced: process names, users, key paths) ran out of its 60 s deadline or failed: the rows are gone,
the strings stay until the weekly sweep or a rerun of the purge (the rerun is idempotent and finishes the sweep), the
reply carries a `constrained` result status (`echo:purge_dictionary_pending`) and `dict_gc_starved_total` is
incremented, so the response record never claims a complete erasure the dictionary sweep has not finished: a pending
result is not a complete erasure. Two limits: the server's `echo.source.purge` audit row is written at dispatch and
carries no agent reply (the reply is in the command's response record), and a write-ahead-log checkpoint that finds
the file busy after the purge still replies `purged` while the deleted pages stay in the log until the next
checkpoint (a warning is logged). A query over a retired `$<Source>_Live` name (`sql`) answers no rows with a
`constrained` result status, so an empty answer is not mistaken for "nothing happened"; only the status enum reaches
the server, and the retired table's name (`retired_table:<name>`) is in the agent's command log line.

**Empty-result / not-yet-collected convention.** A `planned` leg (see Capture sources by OS) ships
its schema and config key with no collector, so its `$..._*` tables stay queryable and empty,
which means "not yet collecting", never "nothing happened". `module` is the clearest case: Windows
has a collector (ETW), Linux and macOS do not. The `registry` source is `unsupported` off Windows:
the Windows registry does not exist there, so it records nothing and `compatibility` says so.

where_the_data_goes: **Instruction result, primarily.** `status`/`query`/`export`/`sql`/`compatibility` rows travel over the agent's mTLS gRPC channel as the command response and land in the ResponseStore, queryable at `/api/responses/{id}` and rendered by the `/echo` dashboard (`docs/echo-dashboard.md`, `docs/echo-implementer.md`).

**`fleet_snapshot`** feeds the server-side `FleetTopologyStore` on a cache miss, assembling the 3D `/viz/fleet` topology view (the `fleet_snapshot` definition in `echo.yaml`); it is not itself a warehouse read.

**`rollup`/`purge_source`** mutate `echo.db` directly (retention, byte budget, dictionary sweep, source purge) — their effect is visible through later `status`/`query`/`sql` reads, not a separate sink.

**Not consumed by** daily-sync inventory, DEX, or metrics — Echo has no `/metrics` endpoint; `status`'s retention-guard counters are the plugin's only fleet-readable health signal (`do_status` in `echo_plugin.cpp` and `format_retention_guard_lines` in `echo_aggregator.hpp`).

**Sensitivity.** `user` events name the logged-in account; `process` events carry the invoking user and, on Linux only, the command line (Windows and macOS capture names only; where a command line is kept it is redacted only against the configured `*password*`-style substring patterns); `network`/`arp` events carry remote IP/MAC addresses (device identifiers) and the owning `process_name`; the `software` source is an installed-software inventory (name/publisher/version) reachable via `query type=software`/`sql`; `dns`/`mapdrive` add resolved hostnames and mapped-drive usernames/remote hosts; `removable` events name an attached device's vendor/product/serial and its BSD/udev device name; `registry` rows hold the new data (first 512 bytes) of every added or changed watched value, unmasked, with its type and the image of the writing process when attributed; the old value is not kept.

**Siblings:** `crossplatform.echo.*` (this plugin) is standalone; the `installed_software` daily-sync source (ADR-0016) is a separate, machine-scope inventory feed, distinct from Echo's `software` capture source.

**MCP / REST.** Discover: `discover_plugins` (summary) → `yuzu://plugin-docs` (this page as data) → `discover_instructions` / `get_definition("crossplatform.echo.status")`. Run: `execute_instruction {definition_id, parameters}`. Read: `/api/responses/{id}`, and `/viz/fleet` for `fleet_snapshot`.
